texts: good. mire-essence is typed as an oil with 'thick' and 'dark' kept as separate properties, and the compound keeps its essence genus.

bad: two things go wrong -- the bare substance name as the subject of a verb produced one flat event about the kind itself instead of the rule form that reaches actual portions of essence, and 'smells' has no carrier, so 'metallic' is improvised onto the smelling event. Make the smell the subject of a plain 'is' sentence: 'The smell of mire-essence is faintly metallic.' That puts the smell, the metallic quality and the 'faintly' all in slots the translator handles cleanly.

bad: the blended shade was pulled apart into three separate properties, so the parse claims mire-essence is green and, separately, that it is black -- neither of which 'dark green-black' says. Keep the shade as one unbroken term: 'Mire-essence is dark-green-black.'

good. it parses as a fireable per-portion rule with the flame and its 'pale' and 'silver' properties all recorded; the flame is attached as the means of the burning, the nearest slot a 'with'-phrase has.
good. the flame is one typed individual carrying 'pale' and 'silver', tied to mire-essence, and 'mist-light' is kept as a kind of light.

mixed: the parse denies one anonymous substitute rather than denying that any exists, so the universal force of 'no' is lost and a substitute named in a later sentence would not be contradicted. State it as a claim about a whole kind: 'No material can replace mire-essence.'

good. both ingredients hang off the single making event as sources, the compounds decompose correctly ('silken' exposed as a property, the noun modifiers 'mire' and 'sea' left inside their words), and it lands as a fireable per-keeper rule.

bad: with the substance name in subject position the translator wrote one flat event about mire-essence in general rather than the rule form required there, so no actual portion of essence is ever linked to the cauldrons. Turn the sentence around so the cauldrons are the subject: 'The copper cauldrons produce mire-essence.' (Naming the maker works too, and matches the sentence above: 'Keepers draw mire-essence from the copper cauldrons.')
